P001.text: Treat unmet demand and staff capacity at each branch as potentially changing through the year.

P002.text: Counts, attendance, surveys and workload reports measure different aspects of that state; their disagreement does not establish which hours should move.

P003.text: The proposed three-month trial assumes shifts can be rearranged within the existing staffing budget; verify this before launch.

P004.text: Establish repeated baseline observations under current hours, preferably for six weeks, documenting school terms and transport availability.

P005.text: A short baseline may inadequately represent seasonal variation.

P006.text: At each branch, propose a fixed transfer of specified weekday hours to weekend hours, preserving funded staffing hours.

P007.text: Before launch, record the schedule, baseline variation, decision thresholds and workload and service-access guardrails.

P008.text: Throughout the trial, collect daily door counts and program attendance using consistent definitions, record weekly paid hours and staff workload, and repeat the same short demand survey at fixed fortnightly intervals using comparable recruitment across weekday and weekend users and affected nonusers.

P009.text: Record closures, programs, transport changes and school-term status.

P010.text: Review weekly sequences for each branch separately, including total weekly visits, visits in affected time slots, attendance relative to program capacity, reported access difficulties and workload.

P011.text: Examine raw totals alongside rates per open hour so reduced weekday service is not concealed.

P012.text: A proposed benefit rule is at least a 10% increase in total weekly visits over the baseline median in four of the final six weeks, with the sequence also assessed against baseline variation; the 10% threshold is a proposal, not an established meaningful difference.

P013.text: Fix locally meaningful access-loss and workload thresholds before launch.

P014.text: Look for persistent gains, losses, trends, reversals and guardrail crossings across repeated observations.

P015.text: Weekend use alone is insufficient: examine whether total use rises, weekday access deteriorates, unmet-demand reports persist and workload increases.

P016.text: Check whether patterns recur within comparable school-term and transport conditions or coincide with changes in those conditions.

P017.text: Conflicting sequences remain observable evidence rather than being collapsed into a single favorable score.

P018.text: At three months, propose keeping the schedule at a branch only if the predefined benefit rule is met, gains are distinguishable from plausible baseline fluctuation, access and workload guardrails hold, and staffing remains within budget.

P019.text: Propose changing the allocation if repeated evidence identifies useful weekend demand alongside avoidable weekday losses or manageable workload problems; specify the revised hours and repeat measurement after the change.

P020.text: Restore the original schedule if benefits fail the rule or persistent harms outweigh gains.

P021.text: Suspend affected trial hours immediately if safe staffing or the budget cannot be maintained.

P022.text: If evidence remains inconclusive, restore the original schedule pending an explicitly authorized further trial rather than infer success.

P023.text: These sequences can support sustained demand under the tested schedule, but cannot by themselves establish that the schedule caused changes or predict year-round demand.

P024.text: Measurement error, repeat visits, survey selection, regression to the mean, missing observations, seasonal transport and school changes, and altered programming can create apparent trends.

P025.text: Log measurement and intervention changes; analyze periods before and after schedule revisions separately.

P026.text: Avoid treating program attendance and door counts as independent users.

P027.text: If observations are sparse, thresholds prove poorly calibrated or conditions lack comparable coverage, report that uncertainty and identify the additional repeated observations needed.
